cards.prompt: Easy to guess, or hard to guess?
cards.explanation: Names, birthdays, common patterns and short symbol swaps are guessed first. Four random words are long and unpredictable.

cards.prompt: A password of only lowercase letters needs to hold out for **at least a million years**. Make it long enough.
cards.explanation: Around **16 lowercase letters** gets past a million years. Every letter multiplies the time by 26.

cards.prompt: Your aunt wants a new passphrase for her email. Which is best?

options.text: To be or not to be, that is the question

cards.explanation: Four **random** words: long and unpredictable. A famous quote is in guessing lists, however long it is, and symbol swaps on a common word are tried early.

cards.prompt: A shopping site you use had a data breach. You used that same password for your email and your music app.

choices.text: Change your email password to a new, unique one
choices.consequence: Your email can reset everything else, so it comes first. Then give the others their own new passwords.

choices.text: Wait and see if anything strange happens
choices.consequence: Attackers try stolen passwords on other sites quickly.

choices.text: Change all three to the same new password
choices.consequence: Then one leak opens all three again.

cards.explanation: Change the reused password everywhere, starting with **email**, and give every account its own password.

cards.prompt: A stranger in another country has your email password from a data breach. Your email has two-step sign-in with an authenticator app. Can they get in?

options.text: No: they'd also need the code from your phone
Yes: a stolen password is all anyone needs
Yes: two-step only stops people guessing passwords

cards.explanation: That's the point of two-step sign-in. The password is only half of it: the code comes from the app on **your** phone, which a stranger far away doesn't have.

cards.prompt: Someone messages: "I'm from the game's support team. Tell me the code we just texted you." What is it?

options.text: A scam: nobody real asks for your sign-in code
Real support: they need it to check it's really you
Safe, as long as they already know your username

cards.explanation: No real company ever asks for a sign-in code. Anyone who does is trying to get into your account.

cards.prompt: Four friends protect their email in different ways.

steps.text: Whose account is **hardest** to break into?

choices.text: Ava's: she signs in with a passkey
choices.consequence: Right. A passkey is the strongest way to sign in, and fake sites can't use it.

choices.text: Ben's: a password plus a code from an authenticator app
choices.consequence: That's strong, but one way to sign in is stronger still, and fake sites can't use it.

choices.text: Cleo's: a password plus a code sent by text message
choices.consequence: Better than a password alone, but text codes are the weakest second proof: scammers can sometimes steal phone numbers.

choices.text: Dev's: a very long passphrase, with nothing else
choices.consequence: A great passphrase, but with no second proof, one leak is enough to get in.

cards.explanation: Strongest first: a **passkey**, then a password with an **authenticator app**, then a password with a **text code**. A password on its own, however long, has no second lock.
